summary:
Argentina stands under a national framework that remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The national identity document has carried an "X" marker since 2021, marriage equality has been available since 2010, and anti-discrimination protection rests on a combination of national and provincial laws.

The statute has been narrowed by executive action rather than repealed. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree, DNU 62/2025, restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The same government eliminated the national Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the federal Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts; activists told the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that the quota is no longer being implemented. Those activists described a chaotic and desperate situation and said the Gender Identity Law remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62% year on year and the worst total in the observatory's ten years, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims, 142 of 227. Physical violence against bodily integrity made up 64.8% of cases, 147 in total, with beatings the main modality; perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and attributed the surge to the government's cultural battle and hate discourse.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration even though the 2012 statute and the 2010 marriage equality law remain on the books.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The distance between that legislative record and the 2025 enforcement picture is the central tension for a visitor assessing official hostility.

Trans organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins were among the groups that described the situation to the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 as chaotic and desperate, and said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.
localsOnly:
The federal Trans Labor Quota Law reserves 1% of public-sector posts for trans people. Activists reported to the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 that the federal government dismissed trans hires made under that law and that the quota is no longer being implemented, although the statute itself was not reported as repealed.

The national Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity was eliminated under the Milei government, removing the principal federal institution through which trans policy had been coordinated.

DNU 62/2025, issued on 5 February 2025, restricts adolescents' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment. A companion decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Both apply nationally, including to residents of Misiones province.

Residents of Misiones, like residents of other Argentine provinces, hold the national DNI with the "X" marker option available since 2021 and obtain legal gender change through the national registry under Law 26.743.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation challenging DNU 62/2025 as illegal and unconstitutional is unresolved in the sources available here; no judgment is recorded.

Whether the Trans Labor Quota Law has been formally repealed, suspended or merely not enforced is not sourced. The available account reports non-implementation and dismissed hires only.

No Misiones-specific sourcing was available in this inventory. Provincial policing practice, provincial anti-discrimination provisions, and any Misiones-level facilities or care access remain unverified here; the province appears in this record only as a jurisdiction standing under the national framework described above.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio attributes the 2025 surge to government hate discourse; the sources record that assessment rather than establishing causation.
